segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Hello, this is 6 Minute English from BBC Learning English. I'm Phil.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: And I'm Beth.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Grey hairs, wrinkles and poor eyesight are common signs that our body is growing old.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Much as we'd like to, we can't avoid ageing, so it's important to stay healthy as we get older.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: In this programme, we'll be hearing about some new research offering fresh advice on how to stay young at heart, an idiom meaning to keep a youthful outlook on life, whatever your age.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: And of course, we'll be learning some useful new vocabulary as well.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: But 6 Minute English isn't just about vocabulary. We improve your listening skills as well.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: So why not turn on the audio subtitles or download the script to read along as you listen?

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: could also help you answer my question.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: The oldest recorded person ever to have lived

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: was a woman who was born in 1875

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: and lived to the ripe old age of 122.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: But which country was she from?

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Was it A. Japan, B. France or C. Italy?

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Oh, I am going to say Japan.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: OK, Beth, I'll reveal the correct answer later in the programme.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Aging is partly caused by the body cells starting to decay so you might think we powerless to stop it But listen to this good news from Professor Sarah Harper director of the Oxford Institute of Population Ageing

segments.speaker: Prof Sarah Harper
segments.text: I think the really exciting thing is that even 10 years ago,

segments.speaker: Prof Sarah Harper
segments.text: we would have thought, yes, it's all to do with our cells.

segments.speaker: Prof Sarah Harper
segments.text: Now we understand this relationship between what we call cell and society,

segments.speaker: Prof Sarah Harper
segments.text: and we really can make a difference.

segments.speaker: Prof Sarah Harper
segments.text: And in fact, a recent paper just came out which said that 60% of our ageing

segments.speaker: Prof Sarah Harper
segments.text: can be controlled by how we live.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Professor Harper says that 60% of ageing is determined by something we can influence, our lifestyle.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: So what lifestyle should we choose?

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Here's Sarah Harper giving more details to BBC Radio 4 programme Inside Health.

segments.speaker: Prof Sarah Harper
segments.text: You know, there's obviously things like diet, which I think we'll come to, but there's also a positive attitude.

segments.speaker: Prof Sarah Harper
segments.text: And there's been some wonderful twin studies that have been done where you've had twins and they have been able to map them across their lives.

segments.speaker: Prof Sarah Harper
segments.text: And if you're positive, you actually have far greater health in later life than if you're negative.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: One important factor in ageing well is a positive attitude,

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: feeling hopeful, confident and focused on the good things in life.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: This conclusion was based on several twin studies,

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: scientific research which uses twins to study the roles of genetics and environment in human development.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: In studies, Professor Harper found positive twins stayed healthier than negative twins

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: as they aged.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Loneliness can be another problem as we get older Here Professor Sarah Harper explains how in countries like Spain Italy and Greece regular social interaction helps people age well

segments.speaker: Prof Sarah Harper
segments.text: Loneliness can have the same impact as smoking in the statistics

segments.speaker: Prof Sarah Harper
segments.text: And when we talked about the Mediterranean diet, it's also got two other sides.

segments.speaker: Prof Sarah Harper
segments.text: It's got exercise because these people tend to be outside more because they have that kind of a climate.

segments.speaker: Prof Sarah Harper
segments.text: But also they still tend to live...

segments.speaker: Prof Sarah Harper
segments.text: Camino meals.

segments.speaker: Prof Sarah Harper
segments.text: Absolutely. They have communal meals, they tend to live together more in multi-generational households.

segments.speaker: Prof Sarah Harper
segments.text: That is changing a bit. So there's a whole lifestyle around it.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: The healthy food, such as fresh vegetables and fish,

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: eaten by people living in countries around the Mediterranean Sea, is known as the Mediterranean diet.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Mediterranean cultures have other advantages too, including outdoor exercise,

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: which is easier in warm climates, and communal meals, occasions where people sit down and share

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: food together.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Mediterranean people are also more likely to live in multi-generational households,

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: where people from two or more generations of a family live together in the same house.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Not everyone can live in the Mediterranean, but it seems a positive attitude and social

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: interaction are two things we can all do to age well. Speaking of which, what was the answer

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: to your question, Phil?

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: OK well I asked you about the oldest living person ever recorded I asked what country they came from and you said Japan Well I can reveal the answer is actually France A lady in France lived for 122 years and 164 days And if you knew the answer to that

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: there are other questions about this programme in the quiz on our worksheet, which you can find on

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: our website, bbclearningenglish.com. Okay, let's recap the new vocabulary we've learnt about staying

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: young at heart, an idiom which means to think and behave in a youthful way in spite of growing older.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: People with a positive attitude feel hopeful, confident and focused on the good things in life.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Twin studies use twins to investigate the roles of genetics and environment in human development.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: A Mediterranean diet describes the foods typically eaten by people living in countries

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: around the Mediterranean Sea, including fresh vegetables, olive oil and fish.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: At a communal meal, people sit down together to talk and share food.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: And finally, a multi-generational household is when people from two or more generations

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: of the same family live together.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: Once again, our six minutes are up.

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: But if you enjoyed this discussion, then head over to the BBC Learning English website

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: to find the accompanying worksheet and quiz,

segments.speaker: Beth
segments.text: along with loads of other programmes and resources to help you learn English.

segments.text: See you there.

segments.speaker: Phil
